name: Fentanyl
summary: Fentanyl's reputation is for potency, but the thing that catches people is its shape. A single dose wears off in half an hour — not because it has been cleared, but because it has moved into tissue. Give it again and the tissue fills up, and the drug that lasted thirty minutes starts lasting many hours. Its duration depends on how long you have been taking it.
mechanism: A highly fat-soluble full mu agonist, roughly a hundred times more potent than morphine by weight. The fat-solubility is why it reaches the brain in under a minute and why it then vanishes into muscle and fat just as quickly. Unusually among opioids it also causes chest-wall rigidity at high doses, which can make rescue breathing physically difficult.

two_compartment.note: The tissue compartment is roughly seven times the blood compartment. Watch the peripheral bar in the body view fill during repeated doses — that filling is exactly what turns a short drug into a long one.

iv.note: Effect within a minute. The clinical duration of a single dose is about 30-60 minutes, which is redistribution into tissue, not elimination — the drug is still in the body, just not in the blood.

insufflated.note: Rapid and near-complete absorption across the nasal mucosa.

smoked.note: Very fast; losses to the vapour stream are substantial and variable.

transdermal.note: The patch is a deliberate flip-flop design: it releases far more slowly than the body clears, so the level is set by the patch, not by metabolism. It takes 12-24 hours to reach a steady level and, critically, a similar time to fall after removal — taking the patch off does not end the dose. Heat raises absorption sharply, which is why fever, hot baths and heating pads have caused fatal overdoses.

pathways.name: Norfentanyl
pathways.note: Inactive, and the usual marker in toxicology.

effect_levels.label: 2 µg/L — marked respiratory depression in the non-tolerant
5 µg/L — range commonly reported in fatalities

risk: The doses here are in fractions of a milligram. Two milligrams can be fatal to someone without tolerance — an amount too small to see clearly, let alone divide evenly. This is why contaminated supply is so lethal: the difference between a dose and an overdose is smaller than the error in mixing.

Context-sensitive half-time is the trap. Add several doses to the timeline and watch how much longer the later ones take to fall. Someone who has been using for hours is not dealing with the same drug they started with.
Onset is fast enough that an overdose can progress before anyone notices anything is wrong, which removes the window in which a slower opioid would be survivable.
Chest-wall rigidity at high doses can prevent effective rescue breathing.
Naloxone works, but high-potency exposure may need repeated doses, and fentanyl outlasts it — observation after reversal is essential.
Patches contain a large reservoir even after use, and heat increases delivery.
